scenes.title: Cold open
narration: The Living Architecture of Algemesí
This is Muixeranga. 18th century to present.
on_screen: Title card: Muixeranga · Spain · 18th century to present

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The tradition is rooted in the 'moixiganga', a series of human tower dances once found across the Iberian Peninsula.
While some theories suggest the name derives from the Arabic 'mochain' (mask), others link it to ancient street processions.
The first solemn celebrations in Algemesí occurred in 1724, and the tradition was nearly lost by 1973 before being revived by local citizens.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The primary occasion is the festival of the Virgin of Health in Algemesí on September 7 and 8.
It is a religious, community-based ritual that has evolved from guild-based participation to a broader social activity.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Performers dance in two rows before transitioning into human towers.
The towers are built to form specific figurative shapes.
A master coordinates the group.
Watch for Tower construction.
on_screen: Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Two rows for the initial dance; dense, circular human tower for the figures.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Listen for the tabalet (drum), dolçaina (shawm).
The music is defined by the piercing, high-pitched, and loud sound of the dolçaina, supported by the steady, rhythmic beat of the tabalet drum.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Performers wear shirts and trousers with vertical red and blue stripes on a white base, reminiscent of harlequin patterns.
Historically, these were made from recycled mattress fabric.
The setting is the street procession during the Mare de Déu de la Salut festival.
on_screen: Image gallery: 2 licensed images with attribution
Reconstruction imagery allowed only from the costume notes, labelled 'reconstruction'

scenes.title: The people
narration: Tomàs Pla, Martí Domínguez i Barberà, and the 1973 revival group members.
Enric Cabrera is remembered as a long-term master.
Variants include the 'Ball de Valencians' (historical), 'Els Negrets de l'Alcúdia', and various 'Noves Muixerangues' formed in the 21st century.
The Muixeranga is considered the historical ancestor of the modern Catalan 'castells'.
